To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
lower IL-4, lower IL-12 and lower IL-10 in peripheral blood monocytes are risk factors for the development of TB in early HIV infection.
lower IL-4, lower IL-12, and lower IL-13 in peripheral blood monocytes are associated with the development of tuberculosis in HIV-infected individuals.

HIV+TB+ individuals have lower levels of interleukins IL-12 and IL-10 and lower expression of Th1 and Th 2 cytokines in unstimulated and stimulated peripheral blood mononucleated cells compared to HIV+ TB- individuals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new approach to the study of HIV and tuberculosis.
the development of new strategies for the early diagnosis of TB in HIV patients.
understanding the mechanisms of susceptibility to tuberculosis in HIV-infected individuals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
IL-12 is a key cytokine in the immune response to TB and that its deficiency is associated with increased susceptibility to TB, especially among HIV-infected patients.
IL-12p40 and Th1/Th2 cytokines are involved in the pathogenesis of TB in HIV infection and may serve as markers for TB development.
the lower levels of interleukine-12 precede development of TB among HIV-infected patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HIV-infected individuals are at high risk of developing TB even in the presence CD4(+) counts in the normal range.
HIV+ individuals with low IL-12 production in response to TB antigen stimulation are at increased risk of developing TB.
the development of TB in women with HIV is associated with a lower level of Th2 cytokine expression in PBMC and lower expression of IL12(p35) by stimulated PBMC cultures.
The main takeaway from our work is that
lower levels of IL-12 precede TB in women.
the immune response to tuberculosis in HIV-infected individuals is more complex than previously thought.
the immune response of HIV+TB+ individuals is different than the immune response of healthy controls.
